name: csvkit
purpose: Suite of command-line tools for converting to and working with CSV: format conversion, SQL querying, joining, statistics, searching and cleaning, designed to compose in a shell pipeline.
journalism_use_case: The data journalist's shell toolkit: convert a government Excel release to CSV, inspect its columns and types, query it with SQL, join it to another release and produce summary statistics — all without opening a spreadsheet or writing a script, which is how most newsroom data work actually starts.
pros: Composable command-line design means a data-cleaning recipe is a shell pipeline you can save, share and rerun — reproducibility for people who would never write Python
csvstat and csvlook give immediate, honest visibility into a dataset's shape and problems, which is the step reporters most often skip
Written by and for data journalists (the wireservice lineage), so the tools match newsroom problems rather than general data engineering
MIT licensed with a long track record and wide packaging
cons: Performance on very large files is poor: csvkit loads and processes in ways that become impractical above a few hundred megabytes, where you want DuckDB or VisiData instead
Maintenance cadence has slowed considerably over the years, with development now largely corrective rather than feature-adding
Type inference can surprise: it will guess a column is numeric or a date and silently change your data's meaning, which matters when a leading-zero identifier becomes an integer
Shell-only, so it suits terminal-comfortable users and excludes others
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived with a long release history and slowed recent development. csvkit's standing in data journalism is well established through the wireservice ecosystem and its presence in the field's teaching materials.
assessment: Adopt it for the quick inspect-convert-join work that constitutes most newsroom data handling, and switch to DuckDB or VisiData above a few hundred megabytes. For your profile the specific hazard to teach is type inference: run csvstat first, and when a column holds identifiers with leading zeros or long numbers, force it to text, because a silently mangled identifier column has produced published errors before.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived with a long release history and reduced recent activity. A mature, feature-complete toolkit where low velocity reflects completion rather than neglect, though it means performance limitations will not be addressed.
costs: No fee. Negligible resources for files it handles comfortably.
alternatives: DuckDB for the same SQL-over-CSV capability at much larger scale
VisiData for interactive terminal exploration
xsv or qsv for high-performance CSV processing

name: DuckDB spatial extension
purpose: Spatial extension for DuckDB providing geometry types, spatial functions, spatial joins and reading of common geospatial formats directly in SQL, inside an embedded analytical database.
journalism_use_case: SQL over large datasets including geospatial ones, on a laptop: query a multi-gigabyte procurement extract, join it to administrative boundaries, and aggregate by region — the analysis that would otherwise need a PostGIS server or exceed pandas' memory.
pros: Embedded means no server: a multi-gigabyte spatial join runs in a laptop process, which removes the infrastructure barrier that keeps newsrooms away from larger datasets
Reads Parquet, CSV, GeoJSON and shapefiles directly in SQL, so the ETL step often disappears entirely
MIT licensed with very active development (pushed 2026-11-12) backed by DuckDB Labs
SQL is the lingua franca a mixed team can share, and the queries are a reproducible methodology artefact
cons: 133 open issues and a pre-1.0 extension line (tag v0.9.1): the spatial extension is less mature than DuckDB core, and function coverage against PostGIS is incomplete
No release objects, so pinning means tracking DuckDB versions and extension compatibility, which is a real operational annoyance
Spatial function semantics differ subtly from PostGIS in places, so a query ported from one to the other may produce different results without erroring
Embedded model means no concurrent multi-user access, so it is an analysis tool rather than a shared database
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 723 stars with 133 open issues, no release objects, latest tag v0.9.1, pushed 2026-11-12, MIT licence. DuckDB's broader adoption in data journalism is well established; the spatial extension is newer and correspondingly less proven.
assessment: Adopt DuckDB generally and use the spatial extension where it covers what you need, verifying results against QGIS or geopandas on a sample before trusting a large spatial join — the maturity gap against PostGIS is real. For your profile the combination that removes most infrastructure from data work is DuckDB plus Parquet plus Datasette for sharing: a few gigabytes of procurement or registry data becomes queryable and publishable without a server.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-12, no release objects, latest tag v0.9.1, 723 stars, 133 open issues. Current commits under DuckDB Labs; the pre-1.0 extension versioning and backlog indicate an area still maturing.
costs: No fee. Runs in-process; RAM and disk proportional to data. Among the cheapest ways to handle large data. Estimate.
privacy: Entirely local, in-process, no network. Excellent for sensitive datasets on an isolated machine.
alternatives: PostGIS where spatial function completeness and multi-user access matter
geopandas for Python-native spatial analysis at smaller scale
QGIS for interactive verification of spatial results

name: Zingg
purpose: Spark-based entity-resolution and identity-graph tool using active learning to train match models, with blocking, deduplication and linking across large datasets.
journalism_use_case: Entity resolution at a scale beyond Splink's comfortable range: linking tens of millions of records across several large datasets — a national property register against a company registry against a sanctions list — where Spark's distribution is the only practical route.
pros: Spark backend means genuinely large-scale resolution is possible, which is the specific gap above Splink's DuckDB comfort zone
Active learning reduces the labelling burden, so a domain expert trains the matcher with a manageable number of judgements
Open-source core with documentation oriented to practical deployment rather than research
Addresses identity-graph construction, which is the shape of the problem in cross-dataset investigation
cons: Spark is a heavy operational dependency: for most newsroom datasets it is unjustified overhead, and standing up a cluster to resolve a few million records is the wrong trade
Commercial product behind the open core, so feature availability and direction follow the vendor — check what is in the open version before designing around it
Smaller community than Splink in the investigative and public-sector space, so there is less accumulated guidance for this kind of data
Match-quality interpretation is the same hard problem as any entity resolution, and Spark's distance from the data makes iterative inspection less convenient than DuckDB-backed Splink
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived. Zingg is positioned as an enterprise entity-resolution tool with an open core; I verified no journalism deployment, so newsroom use is unestablished.
assessment: Consider it only if your record volumes genuinely exceed what Splink handles on a single machine — which for most newsroom work they will not, since Splink is comfortable into the tens of millions with DuckDB. For your profile I would default to Splink for the auditability and the absence of Spark, and keep Zingg in mind for the exceptional case of a very large multi-dataset linkage project, ideally with a data-engineering partner.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived, but with an open-core commercial model where the relationship between the published repository and the commercial product is not clear from metadata alone. Classified Uncertain because open-core projects can quietly shift capability to the paid tier, and this survey did not assess that.
licence: AGPL-3.0 (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file; open-core model with a separate commercial offering)
licence_restrictions: AGPL-family copyleft on the open core would affect offering a modified service. More importantly, verify which capabilities are in the open version versus the commercial product before designing around it.
costs: Open core free. Spark cluster infrastructure is the real cost and it is substantial relative to single-machine alternatives. Commercial product priced separately (not verified). Estimate.
privacy: Self-hosted Spark keeps data on your infrastructure; a cloud Spark deployment moves it to that provider.
alternatives: Splink — recommended: auditable match weights, DuckDB backend, no Spark, actively maintained
nomenklatura where data is already in FollowTheMoney
dedupe for small analyst-driven jobs, with its maintenance caveat
blockers: Spark dependency is disproportionate for most newsroom volumes; open-core capability boundary unverified

name: Leaflet
purpose: Lightweight JavaScript library for interactive maps, with tile-layer support, vector overlays, markers, popups and a large plugin ecosystem, designed to work on mobile and in constrained environments.
journalism_use_case: Publishing an interactive map with a story: incident locations, a procurement geography, a flight path — rendered in the reader's browser with a small library that works on low-end devices and slow connections, which matters for audiences in the regions exile media serve.
pros: Very small and dependency-free, so it loads on poor connections and old devices — a real editorial consideration for audiences outside wealthy markets
BSD-2-Clause with an enormous ecosystem (45,950 stars) and plugins for clustering, heatmaps and most newsroom needs
Simple API that a front-end developer learns in an afternoon, so a map is hours of work rather than a project
Still actively developed (pushed 2026-11-17) with a 2.0 beta line after a long stable period
cons: Release cadence is slow: the stable release v1.9.4 dates from 2023-05-18 with v2.0.0-beta.4 tagged since, so you choose between a three-year-old stable release and a beta
Raster-tile oriented by design; large vector datasets and smooth zooming are MapLibre's territory, not Leaflet's
Default tile layers point at third-party providers (OpenStreetMap or commercial), so every reader's map viewport is reported to that provider — a reader-privacy issue most newsrooms never consider
219 open issues; plugin quality varies enormously and many popular plugins are unmaintained
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 45,950 stars with 219 open issues, stable release v1.9.4 (2023-05-18), tag v2.0.0-beta.4, pushed 2026-11-17, BSD-2-Clause. The long gap between the stable release and current development is visible in the API data.
assessment: Adopt it for most newsroom maps — the loading-weight advantage is decisive when your audience is on constrained connections, and the API is quick enough that maps actually get made. For your profile the under-considered issue is reader privacy: self-host your tiles (PMTiles plus a static host) rather than loading from a third-party provider, because otherwise every reader of a sensitive story reports their map interactions to someone else. Decide deliberately between the stable release and the 2.0 beta.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, stable release v1.9.4 (2023-05-18), tag v2.0.0-beta.4, 45,950 stars, 219 open issues. Current commits on a 2.0 line but no stable release in three years — a mature library in a slow major-version transition.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Map tiles carry the tile provider's licence and attribution requirements (OpenStreetMap tiles require ODbL attribution).
licence_restrictions: Library permissive. Attribution obligations attach to the tiles and data you display, which is a real publication requirement rather than a formality.
costs: No fee. Tile serving is the cost: third-party providers have usage limits and paid tiers (not priced here), while self-hosted PMTiles on static storage is nearly free. Estimate.
privacy: Client-side rendering, but tile requests go to whichever provider you configure, disclosing each reader's map viewport and interaction pattern to that provider. Self-hosting tiles removes this and is the recommended configuration for sensitive stories.
alternatives: MapLibre GL JS for vector tiles and smooth zooming at greater weight
PMTiles plus tippecanoe to self-host tiles and remove the third-party dependency
A static image map where interactivity adds nothing

name: MapLibre GL JS
purpose: WebGL-based vector-tile map rendering library, the community fork of Mapbox GL JS from before its licence change, supporting styled vector tiles, 3D terrain and smooth continuous zoom.
journalism_use_case: Publishing maps where the data is large or the styling matters: thousands of incident points with smooth zoom, a custom cartographic style matching your publication's design, or terrain rendering for a conflict-geography explainer.
pros: Vector tiles handle large datasets and arbitrary zoom far better than raster approaches, so a map with tens of thousands of features stays usable

BSD-3-Clause (licence resolved in this survey; GitHub reports NOASSERTION) — the fork exists precisely because Mapbox moved to a restrictive licence, so this is the licence-safe lineage and that history is worth knowing
Very actively maintained (v6.19.0 released 2026-11-17, same-day push) with a substantial community (12,111 stars) and genuine multi-organisation governance
Pairs directly with PMTiles for fully self-hosted vector maps with no tile-server infrastructure
cons: Heavier than Leaflet in both bundle size and GPU requirements, which matters for readers on low-end devices — the opposite trade-off to Leaflet and a real editorial choice
Styling is powerful and complex: producing a good custom style is a design project, not a configuration tweak
296 open issues and a fast major-version cadence, so pinning matters
Requires vector tiles, so you need a tile-production step (tippecanoe) that raster workflows avoid
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 12,111 stars with 296 open issues, release v6.19.0 published 2026-11-17 with same-day push, SPDX NOASSERTION with the licence resolved to BSD-3-Clause by reading the blob (MapLibre contributors copyright). The project's origin as a community fork after Mapbox's licence change is documented by the organisation.
assessment: Adopt it where the map is the story and data volume or styling justifies the weight; choose Leaflet where reach on constrained devices matters more. For your profile the combination worth building once is MapLibre plus tippecanoe plus PMTiles on static storage: it gives you fully self-hosted vector maps with no tile-server to run, no third-party provider seeing your readers, and no licence exposure — which is a durable capability rather than a per-story effort.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v6.19.0 published the same day, 12,111 stars, 296 open issues. Same-day release and commits under multi-organisation community governance.
licence: BSD-3-Clause (licence blob read 2026-11-17, MapLibre contributors; GitHub reports NOASSERTION)
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Tiles and underlying data carry their own licences and attribution requirements.
licence_restrictions: Library permissive — and deliberately so, as the fork exists to escape Mapbox's licence change. Attribution obligations attach to the map data you display.
costs: No fee. Tile production and hosting are the costs; PMTiles on static storage is close to free. Estimate.
privacy: Client-side rendering; tile requests go to your configured source. Self-hosted PMTiles keeps reader interactions entirely within your infrastructure, which is the privacy-preserving configuration.
alternatives: Leaflet for lighter maps and better reach on constrained devices
deck.gl or kepler.gl for heavy data-visualisation layers
Static map images where interactivity is not needed

name: tippecanoe
purpose: Command-line tool that builds vector tilesets from large GeoJSON collections, with zoom-dependent feature selection, simplification and attribute handling to keep tiles small.
journalism_use_case: Turning a large geospatial dataset into publishable map tiles: a million property parcels, every incident in a conflict dataset, all procurement locations in a country — tiled so a reader's browser loads only what is in view.
pros: Handles very large feature collections and makes sensible zoom-dependent decisions automatically, which is the hard part of vector-tile production
BSD-2-Clause with active maintenance (pushed 2026-11-16) under Felt's stewardship after the transfer from Mapbox
Produces output consumable by MapLibre and PMTiles, completing a fully self-hosted map pipeline
Deterministic CLI, so tile production is a reproducible build step rather than a manual process
cons: Release cadence has lapsed: release 2.79.0 dates from 2025-07-24 with a non-semantic tag since, so pinning is awkward
The flag surface is large and the defaults are not always what you want for a given dataset — producing good tiles takes iteration and reading the documentation carefully
C++ build or a package install, which is an extra toolchain in an otherwise JavaScript or Python workflow
173 open issues; feature-dropping decisions at low zoom can silently omit data in ways that misrepresent a dataset if you do not check the output
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 1,637 stars with 173 open issues, release 2.79.0 (2025-07-24), pushed 2026-11-16, BSD-2-Clause. The transfer from Mapbox to Felt is reflected in the repository ownership.
assessment: Adopt it as the tile-production step in a self-hosted map pipeline. For your profile the quality check that matters is inspecting the tiles at low zoom: tippecanoe drops features to keep tiles small, and a map that silently omits a third of the incidents at country zoom is editorially wrong even though it looks fine. Set the feature-dropping behaviour deliberately and verify counts at each zoom level before publishing.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release 2.79.0 (2025-07-24), 1,637 stars, 173 open issues. Current commits under Felt's maintenance with a lapsed release cadence; active but with poor release hygiene.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Tiled data carries its source licence and attribution obligations.
costs: No fee. CPU and disk for tile generation — a large dataset is minutes to hours and gigabytes of output. Estimate.
privacy: Entirely local tile generation; no network calls.
alternatives: PMTiles' own tooling for simpler conversions
Planetiler for OpenStreetMap-scale basemap generation
A hosted tile service, accepting the third-party dependency and reader-privacy cost

name: PMTiles
purpose: Single-file archive format for map tiles that supports HTTP range requests, allowing a whole tileset to be served from static storage with no tile server, plus reference implementations in several languages.
journalism_use_case: Self-hosting map tiles with no infrastructure: put one PMTiles file on static storage or a CDN and serve an interactive map, which removes both the tile-server operations and the third-party tile provider that would otherwise see every reader's map viewport.
pros: Eliminates tile-server infrastructure entirely — a single file on static hosting is the cheapest and most durable way to publish maps, and it keeps working long after a story is published
Removes the reader-privacy problem: no third-party tile provider sees your audience's map interactions, which matters for sensitive stories
Licence resolved in this survey and unusually favourable: BSD-3-Clause for the reference implementations and the SPECIFICATION ITSELF IS PUBLIC DOMAIN / CC0 — so the format carries no lock-in at all
Very clean tracker (19 open issues against 3,233 stars) and an established maintainer in the open-mapping space
cons: Last push 2026-09-16 with no release objects at all, so pinning means tracking commits — modest risk for a format implementation, but poor release hygiene
Requires tile production upstream (tippecanoe or Protomaps' own tooling), so it is one component of a pipeline rather than a complete solution
HTTP range requests must be supported by your hosting, which most static hosts do but some configurations break
Bundled sample tilesets in the repository have their own licence terms, as the licence file notes — a detail to check if you use them
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 3,233 stars with 19 open issues, no release objects, pushed 2026-09-16, SPDX NOASSERTION with the licence blob read 2026-11-17 stating BSD-3-Clause for the reference implementations, the specification in the public domain or CC0, and separate terms for sample tilesets.
assessment: Adopt it as the default way to publish maps — the combination of no server, no third-party tile provider and a public-domain specification is as close to a free lunch as this catalogue contains. For your profile the pipeline to build once is tippecanoe to tiles, PMTiles as the archive, static storage to serve, MapLibre or Leaflet to render. After that, every map is a build step rather than a project, and no reader's viewport leaves your infrastructure.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-09-16, no release objects, 3,233 stars, 19 open issues. Two months since last push with a very clean tracker; a format specification plus reference implementations, where stability is appropriate and the public-domain specification insulates you from maintainer risk.
licence: BSD-3-Clause for the reference implementations; the PMTiles SPECIFICATION is public domain or CC0 where applicable; bundled sample tilesets have their own terms (licence blob read 2026-11-17; GitHub reports NOASSERTION)
model_or_data_licence: Sample tilesets in the repository are subject to their own licence terms, as the licence file states explicitly.
licence_restrictions: Essentially none: implementations are permissive and the format itself is unencumbered, so there is no lock-in risk. Check the terms of any bundled sample tileset you use.
costs: No fee. Static storage for the tile archive — pennies per month for a national-scale tileset on object storage. The cheapest map-publishing path available. Estimate.
privacy: Serving from your own static storage means no third-party provider sees reader map requests — the strongest reader-privacy position for interactive maps, and the main non-cost reason to adopt it.
alternatives: A tile server (martin, tileserver-gl) where dynamic tile generation is genuinely needed
MBTiles plus a server for the older equivalent workflow
Commercial tile providers, accepting cost and reader-privacy exposure
